<reason>Both sides were disciplined, well-grounded, and responsive, making this close. PRO's best weapon—the asymmetry frame (platforms exploit 2 a.m. traces commercially with no audit while public science is held to perfection)—was pressed consistently and crystallized well. But CON absorbed it with a coherent alternative (data minimization, restricting profiling, regulator subpoenas with judicial review) rather than pure status quo defense. Meanwhile, CON's rare-trajectory dilemma forced PRO into the tiered-access concession, which CON then collapsed decisively: noise governs only what leaves the room, not what insiders see raw. CON's viewpoint-licensing disanalogy (crash tests measure broken bones; "polarization" measures viewpoints) was never substantively answered by PRO's IRB analogy, and the minors' consent point survived largely intact. CON's rebuttals did more damage per exchange, and both closings were vivid. PRO kept it razor-thin via the asymmetry and "you cannot restrict what you cannot measure," but CON neutralized more of the opponent's core route than vice versa.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.3's collapse of tiered access: PRO conceded rare-trajectory research requires raw sequences inside secure rooms, and CON drove home that differential privacy only polices outputs—"noise on what leaves the room does nothing for what is seen inside it"—converting PRO's fix into a concession that the most sensitive questions require exactly the exposure CON had warned about.</best_rebuttal>
